Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land consists of rectangular or polygonal field parcels separated by crisp visible boundaries.
Annual Crop Land shows a mosaic of neighboring plots with clearly different brown, tan, and green tones.
Annual Crop Land often includes bare-soil parcels beside vegetated parcels, creating strong contrast between adjacent fields.
Annual Crop Land has strong human-imposed geometric regularity, with straight field edges and aligned parcel rows.
Annual Crop Land displays fine, uniform texture within each field while textures change sharply from one parcel to the next.
Annual Crop Land is crossed by narrow farm roads or tracks that run straight along field boundaries.
Annual Crop Land commonly contains drainage or irrigation lines forming linear patterns parallel to plot edges.
Annual Crop Land lacks the repeated dot or grid pattern of tree crowns that marks Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land has low vegetation cover that does not form the dense dark canopy typical of Forest.
Annual Crop Land appears more sharply divided into cultivated units than the broader, less structured grassy areas of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land shows medium to large parcels arranged in an orderly patchwork rather than irregular natural patches.
Annual Crop Land often has alternating light and dark strips caused by different surface conditions in adjacent fields.
Annual Crop Land usually has open, exposed surfaces with little shadow, unlike taller woody vegetation classes.
Annual Crop Land may include isolated small buildings or farm compounds, but built structures remain sparse compared with the field area.
Annual Crop Land has parcel boundaries that meet at straight angles or clean intersections, reinforcing the planned layout.
Annual Crop Land shows managed vegetation distributed evenly within plots rather than continuous wild herbaceous cover.
Annual Crop Land may include small canals or ditches, but open water is limited and secondary to the field pattern.
Annual Crop Land often presents seasonal patchiness, with some plots nearly bare and others covered by short uniform crops.
Annual Crop Land has edge-aligned access routes that create a rectilinear network across the cultivated area.
Annual Crop Land maintains a cultivated patchwork appearance with low canopy and clear parcel separation, unlike Forest or Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings feature very large rectangular roof blocks that occupy broad parcels within built-up areas.
Industrial Buildings show clusters of long warehouse or factory halls arranged with strong rectilinear geometry.
Industrial Buildings contain extensive gray, white, or dark impervious surfaces dominating the patch.
Industrial Buildings are surrounded by broad paved yards or loading aprons that are much wider than those around Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings have building footprints spaced farther apart than the tight small-unit pattern of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings are connected by wide access roads and internal service lanes rather than a single narrow linear corridor like Highway or Road.
Industrial Buildings form organized blocky complexes with sharp edges and right-angled boundaries.
Industrial Buildings usually include large parking or storage surfaces adjacent to the main roofs.
Industrial Buildings have sparse, fragmented vegetation limited to edges or small strips between paved areas.
Industrial Buildings lack the repetitive field textures and seasonal plot patterns seen in Annual Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings lack the evenly spaced orchard rows or tree grids that distinguish Permanent Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings often appear as contiguous industrial estates where multiple oversized roofs sit side by side.
Industrial Buildings show a high proportion of built roof area combined with open paved space, not the garden-like mix of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings commonly have flat-toned surfaces with little internal texture compared with cropland mosaics.
Industrial Buildings occupy compact urban patches whose boundaries are shaped by roads and lots rather than by irregular natural edges.
Industrial Buildings frequently include open hardstand areas for storage that appear as empty rectangular pads beside structures.
Industrial Buildings present a block-dominant pattern where building masses outweigh the visual presence of streets.
Industrial Buildings rarely contain water features, with the patch mostly filled by roofs, pavement, and small vegetation fragments.
Industrial Buildings often align several large roofs parallel to one another within a planned layout.
Industrial Buildings show fewer but much larger structures than Residential Buildings, creating a coarse-grained built pattern.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings consists of many small to medium rectangular roofs packed into neighborhood-sized blocks.
Residential Buildings shows houses aligned along short local streets and cul-de-sacs rather than a few massive building halls.
Residential Buildings has a fine-grained mix of gray roofs, pale pavement, and small green yards.
Residential Buildings forms a regular parcel pattern with repeated lot divisions and closely spaced structures.
Residential Buildings contains narrower roads serving clusters of homes rather than broad pavement dominating the patch.
Residential Buildings displays scattered trees and lawn patches interwoven with buildings, creating a mottled urban texture.
Residential Buildings usually has sharper block edges and more geometric organization than surrounding natural vegetation.
Residential Buildings presents a denser roof pattern than cropland, without long parallel planting rows.
Residential Buildings lacks the large uniform field parcels of Annual Crop Land and instead breaks into many small residential lots.
Residential Buildings has less continuous open paved area than Industrial Buildings, with roofs and yards interrupting the surface.
Residential Buildings often appears as contiguous neighborhood blocks connected by a branching street network.
Residential Buildings shows repeated right-angled building footprints and driveways arranged in compact residential clusters.
Residential Buildings tends to mix built surfaces with small tree canopies, unlike the cleaner hard-surface expanses of industrial sites.
Residential Buildings has a tighter and more intricate internal street pattern than Highway or Road, which is dominated by long linear corridors.
Residential Buildings commonly includes short driveways and side streets feeding homes on both sides of the road.
Residential Buildings creates a textured pattern of alternating rooftops and vegetation rather than the smooth uniformity of crop fields.
Residential Buildings may include small ponds or drainage features, but water is secondary to the dense housing pattern.
Residential Buildings typically fills the patch with closely spaced structures of similar scale rather than isolated large complexes.
Residential Buildings shows neighborhood geometry with curved or rectilinear streets enclosing housing clusters and small yards.
Residential Buildings is characterized by a compact urban fabric where roofs, streets, and scattered trees are balanced at a small spatial scale.
Pasture Land: Pasture Land consists of large open parcels of grass cover separated by clear field boundaries.
Pasture Land shows green to yellow-brown tones spread evenly across a parcel without strong color banding.
Pasture Land has a fine, soft vegetation texture that is smoother than the rougher patchiness of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land usually forms irregular to moderately regular enclosure shapes rather than tightly gridded cultivated blocks.
Pasture Land lacks the repeated parallel row patterns that distinguish Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land is more uniformly vegetated across each field and shows less bare-soil contrast than Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land appears as broad continuous grassy areas with sparse or absent tree canopy over most of the parcel.
Pasture Land often lies beside farm tracks or narrow rural roads that trace parcel edges.
Pasture Land contains few buildings, with structures scattered sparsely compared with urban or industrial land.
Pasture Land has a managed open-field layout with boundaries that are clearer than in natural Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land parcels often connect into contiguous grazing blocks rather than fragmented mixed-cover patches.
Pasture Land shows a consistent grass cover density across the field without orchard-like spacing or woody dots.
Pasture Land commonly includes internal fence-line divisions visible as thin straight or gently curving separators.
Pasture Land has a more open surface and much less shadowing than Forest because tall dense trees are mostly absent.
Pasture Land fields often have edge-defined borders against neighboring cropland, woodland, or roads.
Pasture Land presents gentle tonal variation within parcels instead of alternating planted strips or harvest patterns.
Pasture Land is dominated by low vegetation cover with no dense crown texture and no closed canopy.
Pasture Land may include small ponds or drainage lines, but open water occupies only a minor part of the parcel.
Pasture Land shows human-managed parcel geometry that is simpler and more coherent than semi-natural grassland mosaics.
Pasture Land maintains a broad grassy appearance across each enclosure without the seasonal checkerboard contrast common in Annual Crop Land.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road forms a long, narrow corridor that crosses the scene continuously rather than a compact block like buildings.
Highway or Road has fairly uniform width over long distances, unlike rivers that widen, narrow, and curve irregularly.
Highway or Road usually appears gray, white, or dark with a smooth, even surface and little internal texture.
Highway or Road shows straight segments, sharp bends, and engineered intersections that create angular patterns.
Highway or Road often branches into connected junctions, forming a planned network instead of isolated patches.
Highway or Road contrasts strongly with adjacent green or brown land because the paved strip is relatively non-vegetated.
Highway or Road remains thinner than most developed parcels, separating land areas rather than filling them like industrial sites.
Highway or Road commonly runs along settlement edges or through built-up zones as a linear connector between denser structures.
Highway or Road has parallel edges that stay consistent, while riverbanks are usually uneven and naturally sinuous.
Highway or Road may include divided lanes that appear as paired linear strips with a narrow median between them.
Highway or Road often cuts across herbaceous vegetation as a crisp artificial line through a soft-textured field.
Highway or Road lacks the clustered rectangular rooftops that characterize residential or industrial building areas.
Highway or Road can appear as a grid component where multiple straight corridors meet at right angles.
Highway or Road is usually bordered by thin roadside margins or shadows, but the main feature stays a slender line.
Highway or Road extends across large portions of the scene with continuous connectivity instead of ending as a self-contained footprint.
Highway or Road has a homogeneous tone along its length, unlike building zones that show many small tonal variations.
Highway or Road frequently bypasses or bridges water as a direct straight crossing, while the water body itself remains broader and irregular.
Highway or Road may curve gently, but its path is controlled and smooth rather than freely meandering like a river.
Highway or Road separates adjacent land covers into elongated blocks, acting as a boundary line within the urban pattern.
Highway or Road appears as a constructed transport corridor with consistent geometry, not as a textured vegetated patch or broad developed complex.
Forest: Forest shows large contiguous patches of dark green cover rather than many small agricultural parcels.
Forest has a coarse, mottled texture from overlapping tree crowns instead of the smoother surface of herbaceous or pasture land.
Forest forms irregular natural edges that follow terrain or drainage lines, not the straight boundaries common in crop fields.
Forest lacks the repeated row spacing and parallel planting lines typical of permanent crop land.
Forest appears as dense canopy with frequent shadowed pockets inside the patch, unlike the more even brightness of grass-covered land.
Forest contains very few visible internal divisions, in contrast to annual crop land broken into distinct fields.
Forest is dominated by medium to dark green tones with only small interruptions of bare soil or built surfaces.
Forest often has rounded or lobed patch outlines rather than the rectangular blocks common in managed farmland.
Forest shows crown-scale variation in color and texture, not the uniform cover expected in pasture land.
Forest usually has sparse road intrusion, with only occasional narrow tracks crossing the wooded area.
Forest has little to no roof density, unlike developed land with clustered buildings and paved surfaces.
Forest may include narrow winding streams under canopy, but broad open water is not a dominant feature.
Forest follows hillsides and valley shapes with branching margins instead of aligning to a street grid.
Forest presents dense cover that obscures the ground, unlike annual crop land where soil patterns are often visible.
Forest lacks harvest striping or plow marks that create linear banding in cultivated fields.
Forest often contains darker interior zones and lighter edge transitions caused by varying canopy density.
Forest appears less smooth and less uniformly short-textured than herbaceous vegetation land.
Forest forms wooded corridors and blocks connected across the landscape rather than isolated neat plots.
Forest shows natural canopy gaps that are irregularly scattered, not evenly spaced like orchard openings.
Forest has a visually continuous tree layer with minimal geometric repetition compared with permanent crop plantations.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land forms broad open patches with irregular natural outlines rather than neat rectangular field blocks.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows a fine, even grassy texture without the dark coarse canopy pattern of Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land is dominated by green to yellow-brown tones that spread continuously across the surface.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks visible plow lines or parallel row marks that commonly separate Annual Crop Land into strips.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no orchard grid, vine rows, or evenly spaced planting dots typical of Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land appears as continuous low cover with only occasional scattered shrubs or small trees.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land usually has soft-textured vegetation cover with little internal segmentation into paddocks compared with Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains few buildings and no dense rectilinear street network.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land is mostly uninterrupted vegetation surface rather than a mosaic of small enclosed parcels.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land often includes faint narrow tracks but not a strong framework of roads dividing the area into regular lots.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land presents open cover where shadows are limited because tall woody crowns are not dominant.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land tends to have gradual tonal variation across the patch instead of sharp field-by-field contrast.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land occupies sizable areal expanses rather than narrow linear strips along infrastructure.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has a natural mottled grass pattern that is subtler and less repetitive than cultivated planting geometry.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows little to no exposed soil compared with Annual Crop Land during active field preparation.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land commonly borders other land covers with uneven edges instead of straight fence-like boundaries.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land remains visually open, with canopy cover too sparse to create a closed woodland appearance.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land rarely contains water surfaces, and when present they are minor compared with the surrounding vegetation cover.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has low, continuous vegetation density that appears smoother than shrubland and less structured than cropland.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the repeated enclosed pasture compartments and access lanes often visible in managed grazing areas.
River: River forms a long narrow water strip that crosses the scene instead of filling a broad enclosed basin like a lake or sea.
River usually follows a sinuous course with repeated bends rather than the straight engineered alignment of a highway or road.
River often shows branching tributary connections that merge into the main channel.
River has width that changes gradually along its length instead of staying uniformly constant.
River is bounded by irregular natural banks rather than crisp paved edges or lane-marked margins.
River appears as a smooth dark blue, dark green, or gray surface contrasting with rougher surrounding land textures.
River creates a continuous connected water shape rather than many small isolated patches.
River commonly occupies a winding corridor bordered by thin linear bands of vegetation on both sides.
River may spread into a slightly wider reach at bends while remaining elongated overall.
River separates adjacent land-cover patches with a sharply defined dark channel line.
River lacks the internal parallel markings or medians that would suggest a road surface.
River often meanders across floodplain land in looping arcs rather than following a rigid grid.
River can include small side channels or braided threads connected to the main flow.
River tends to have asymmetrical curves and natural edge variation unlike the regular geometry of built infrastructure.
River is darker and smoother than nearby forest, which appears coarse and densely textured.
River narrows into fine upstream segments while remaining linked to wider downstream sections.
River may cut diagonally across fields or urban blocks without matching their geometric orientation.
River often has tapered inlets from tributaries instead of the uniform intersections typical of roads.
River maintains a flowing corridor shape with no roof clusters, street blocks, or dense canopy covering its surface.
River shows elongated water continuity beyond the frame edges, unlike a lake that reads as a contained open-water area.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake shows a broad contiguous water surface occupying a large compact area rather than a narrow elongated channel.
Sea or Lake has a smooth interior with little visible texture compared with the fine mottling of herbaceous vegetation land.
Sea or Lake is dominated by dark blue, blue-green, or gray tones across a wide continuous expanse.
Sea or Lake lacks the rectangular parcel boundaries that organize pasture land into repeated field blocks.
Sea or Lake is enclosed or bordered by a clearly defined shoreline that sharply separates water from adjacent land.
Sea or Lake often forms a rounded, lobed, or irregular basin shape instead of the thin meandering form of a river.
Sea or Lake contains few internal interruptions, with open water extending without the frequent bars or banks seen in rivers.
Sea or Lake may show bright sun-glint patches on part of an otherwise uniform water surface.
Sea or Lake occupies a much greater width-to-length ratio than river features in the same scene.
Sea or Lake has no street grid or dense building footprint pattern within the main water body.
Sea or Lake presents a nearly featureless central area, unlike vegetation classes that show dense textured cover throughout.
Sea or Lake commonly meets land along sweeping curving margins rather than along straight agricultural edges.
Sea or Lake forms a single expansive patch instead of many small adjacent patches typical of managed grassland.
Sea or Lake has shoreline inlets and coves that indent the edge while the interior remains open and unsegmented.
Sea or Lake shows adjacent roads skirting the perimeter rather than crossing repeatedly through the center.
Sea or Lake appears as a large dark tonal mass that contrasts with the lighter mixed tones of surrounding fields or pasture.
Sea or Lake lacks parallel mowing, planting, or grazing traces that can create faint linear texture in grass-covered land.
Sea or Lake may include isolated peninsulas or islands, yet the dominant pattern remains a wide continuous water expanse.
Sea or Lake does not follow a sinuous corridor across the landscape as rivers typically do.
Sea or Lake is characterized by a spacious open-water basin bordered by land on one or more sides without internal field or settlement structure.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land shows large managed parcels with crisp boundaries and a regular internal planting layout.
Permanent Crop Land has rows of evenly spaced woody vegetation forming parallel lines across each field.
Permanent Crop Land often appears as dot-like tree crowns arranged in a consistent grid rather than a smooth grass cover.
Permanent Crop Land displays alternating bands of canopy and bare soil or short ground cover between planted lines.
Permanent Crop Land has a more discrete and patterned texture than Pasture Land or Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Permanent Crop Land contains organized woody cover in rows, unlike Forest which forms a dense continuous canopy.
Permanent Crop Land often uses rectangular or elongated plots with one stable row direction across the whole parcel.
Permanent Crop Land may show terraced strips with repeated planted lines following slope contours.
Permanent Crop Land commonly has internal farm tracks running straight between or along planted blocks.
Permanent Crop Land presents spectral variation by parcel, with each block keeping a uniform row pattern inside it.
Permanent Crop Land frequently includes small repeated canopy clusters separated by visible inter-row gaps.
Permanent Crop Land tends to have medium green to dark green vegetation broken by tan or brown linear soil bands.
Permanent Crop Land shows stronger geometric order than Annual Crop Land, where fields are often more uniformly filled.
Permanent Crop Land often has straight parcel edges aligned with access roads or neighboring planted blocks.
Permanent Crop Land may contain orchard blocks where individual crowns are visible as evenly spaced points.
Permanent Crop Land usually has lower canopy closure than Forest because gaps between planted lines remain visible.
Permanent Crop Land can form long narrow fields whose repeated row texture continues from end to end.
Permanent Crop Land often shows a checkerboard of adjacent plots with different row orientations or canopy densities.
Permanent Crop Land generally has sparse building presence, with the vegetation pattern dominating the parcel structure.
Permanent Crop Land rarely includes broad water surfaces, and when water is present it is secondary to the ordered crop blocks.
